newsitem.title: MEXICO: At last, consumers chip in to Mexican recovery.
newsitem.headline: At last, consumers chip in to Mexican recovery.

text.p: Mexico's consumers are finally opening their pocketbooks after 2-1/2 years of crisis, giving a much needed boost to the recovery of one of Latin America's largest economies, analysts said on Monday.
Recent figures have shown retail sales and industrial production are kicking into gear, while economists expect upcoming trade data to buttress the picture of growth.
But while growth has started to recover, inflation has remained under control.

"It looks like it is not just investment and exports anymore. As exports are becoming less of a contributor, it looks like the consumer is finally starting to contribute," said James Carlin, American Express Financial Services director of economic analysis for emerging markets.

The government said last week that May retail sales rose 4.4 percent compared with the same month a year earlier. That compared with average Reuters forecasts of a 2.3 percent rise and was the second consecutive monthly gain after retail sales fell 3.5 percent in the first quarter.

Other figures released last week showed industrial production up a strong 9.0 percent in May over the same month a year earlier, compared with expectations in a Reuters survey of a rise of 7.88 percent.
"Both May reports (retail sales and industrial production) underscored the strength of the economic recovery and the budding contribution of private consumption," said J.P. Morgan's Alfredo Thorne.
"Plainly, the economy's acceleration is now being led by retailers and producers for the domestic market," Thorne said.
Economists do warn, however, that domestic demand is rebounding from a still weak level.
"There is dynamisn in the economy and that will continue, but there is no consumer boom," said AB Asesores Moneda head of analysis Diego Bravo.
"The consumer is still pretty beaten down. Real wages are still very depressed from where they were before the devaluation," American Express' Carlin added.
Boom or not, economists say data last week and this week will support the contention that gross domestic product grew strongly in the second quarter as the recovery widened to include more sectors.

A survey of 12 brokerages, banks and research firms done by Reuters forecast a rise of 5.42 percent in the second quarter, compared with 5.1 percent in the first quarter. Upgrading of those forecasts was already underway.
A key piece of data, international trade for June, will add another piece to the second quarter GDP picture when it is released this week.
Analysts said it was expected to show continued strength of demand for imports, which is outpacing export growth.
"June trade figures will point up once again that domestic demand and consumption led overall GDP recovery last quarter, with net export demand contributing negatively," said J.P. Morgan's Thorne.
Trade surpluses, one of the brightest spots in the economy since the 1994 peso devaluation, have narrowed recently due to a stubbornly strong peso and rising import demand.
A survey of economists by Reuters found expectations of a preliminary surplus of $164.8 million in June, down from a final surplus of $220 million in May.
Still, despite growing output, there appears to be little pressure on inflation.
The consumer price index in the first half of July -- due to be released on Thursday -- was expected to remain subdued because of a stable peso, high real interest rates and pressure on food prices.
A survey by Reuters found expectations of a rise in CPI of 0.47 percent for the first two weeks in July. In June it rose 0.89 percent -- the second straight month with inflation below 1.0 percent.

Although Mexico's open unemployment rate has also fallen -- to 3.4 percent in June against the 3.9 percent seen in May -- economists say wage recovery has failed to show the same vigor as the jobs market, which means the consumer is still struggling to get above water.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559))
